clinicalPearls: Trismus (lockjaw) is typically the earliest symptom, progressing to neck and trunk rigidity, dysphagia, and pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm; risus sardonicus and opisthotonos reflect the characteristic sustained muscle rigidity.
Generalized tetanus is the most common form, characterized by muscle rigidity with generalized spasms; localized tetanus affects only isolated muscle groups but can progress to the generalized form.
Cephalic tetanus is a localized form involving the cranial nerves, which can cause pharyngeal or laryngeal spasm leading to aspiration, airway obstruction, or respiratory failure.

Neonatal tetanus classically presents with loss of the ability to suck and cry (a newborn normal in the first 2 days who deteriorates between days 3 and 28), poor feeding, rigidity, and generalized spasms.
Laryngeal spasm causing apnea or respiratory failure is a life-threatening event and, without immediate respiratory support, is the most common cause of death.

Autonomic nervous system disturbance characteristically emerges in the second week of severe disease, with fluctuating heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, gastrointestinal stasis, and increased tracheal secretions; cardiovascular events then become the major threat.
Disease severity is graded with the Ablett classification (Grades I-IV), where Grade IV is Grade III plus autonomic dysfunction.
Abdominal rigidity in tetanus is characteristically continuous, distinguishing it from the rigidity of peritonitis or an acute abdomen.

Roughly 20-30% of cases have no identifiable entry wound; superficial limb abrasions are the most common portal of entry in adults, while deeper injuries (open fractures, drug injection) are linked to more severe disease.
Natural infection does not confer protective immunity because tetanus toxin is poorly immunogenic, so survivors still require a full primary immunization course.
harrison.pathophysiology: Tetanus is caused by tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) produced by Clostridium tetani, an anaerobic, gram-positive, spore-forming rod whose resilient environmental spores enter through wounds, abrasions, or the umbilical stump and germinate in anaerobic tissue. Only toxin-producing organisms cause disease. The toxin is a 150-kDa protein cleaved into a heavy (100-kDa) and light (50-kDa) chain joined by a disulfide bond; the heavy-chain carboxy terminal binds presynaptic motor nerve terminals, leading to internalization and retrograde intra-axonal transport to motor nuclei of cranial nerves and spinal cord ventral horns. The toxin then crosses the synapse into GABA-ergic presynaptic inhibitory interneurons, where the light chain (a zinc-dependent endopeptidase) cleaves VAMP2 (synaptobrevin), blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release. Loss of inhibition produces unregulated motor activity (muscle rigidity and spasms), and similar disinhibition in the autonomic system produces autonomic instability; elevated circulating catecholamines in severe disease drive cardiovascular complications.
additionalDifferentials: Dystonic reactions to antidopaminergic (antidopaminergic drug) agents
Oropharyngeal, peritonsillar, or submaxillary infection / lymphadenitis and cranial nerve disease (mimics of cephalic tetanus / trismus)
Peritonitis or acute abdominal emergency (versus continuous abdominal rigidity of tetanus)
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is clinical; confirmatory laboratory testing is limited.
Wound culture of C. tetani cannot confirm the diagnosis (a positive culture is non-confirmatory).
Serum antitetanus IgG measured before antitoxin/immunoglobulin administration: levels >0.1 IU/mL (standard ELISA) are deemed protective and argue against tetanus.
Serum tetanus toxin bioassay may help if antibody is below the protective threshold, but a negative result does not exclude tetanus and the assay is not generally performed.
PCR and recombinase polymerase amplification to detect the tetanus neurotoxin gene are promising but emerging techniques.
redFlags: Laryngeal spasm with apnea or respiratory failure - life-threatening and the most common cause of death.

Autonomic nervous system disturbance (labile heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, GI stasis, increased tracheal secretions), typically in the second week, marking high cardiovascular mortality risk.
Short incubation period (wound to first symptom) and short period of onset (first symptom to first generalized/pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm) - rapid progression predicts worse outcome.
Dysphagia with laryngeal hyperactivity, which makes airway management difficult and raises aspiration risk.
harrison.prognosis: Tetanus has a high survival rate when complications are controlled and interventions are prompt, though recovery is prolonged, typically taking about 4-6 weeks. Rapid onset predicts more severe disease: the shorter the incubation period (wound to first symptom) and the period of onset (first symptom to first generalized or pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm), the worse the prognosis. The Tetanus Severity Score (TSS) outperforms the Dakar and Philips scores for predicting severity and outcome (sensitivity ~66%, specificity ~91%; a cutoff score of >=8 predicts death). Surviving adults, especially the elderly, may have reduced long-term functional outcomes, while affected children and neonates have a higher incidence of neurologic sequelae (neonates may face increased risk of learning disabilities, behavioral problems, cerebral palsy, and deafness).
pitfalls: Diagnosis is clinical - waiting for laboratory confirmation is misguided; a positive wound culture does not confirm and a protective antitetanus IgG (>0.1 IU/mL) argues against the diagnosis.
Treatment should not be delayed once tetanus is clinically diagnosed.
Assuming natural infection confers immunity: tetanus toxin is poorly immunogenic, so survivors still require a full primary immunization course.
Overlooking absence of a wound: about 20-30% of cases have no identifiable entry site, so a negative wound history does not exclude tetanus.
Failure to identify and debride the entry wound (to remove anaerobic foci) can lead to recurrent or prolonged disease.

Long-term ICU care with deep sedation predisposes to hospital-acquired infections (ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream and urinary tract infection, sepsis), venous thromboembolism, and other complications - prognosis depends on controlling these.
harrison.severityClassification: Ablett classification of tetanus severity: Grade I (mild) - mild trismus, general spasticity, no respiratory compromise, no spasms, no dysphagia; Grade II (moderate) - moderate trismus and rigidity, short spasms, mild dysphagia, moderate respiratory involvement, respiratory rate >30/min; Grade III (severe) - severe trismus, generalized rigidity, prolonged spasms, severe dysphagia, apneic spells, pulse >120/min, respiratory rate >40/min; Grade IV (very severe) - Grade III features plus autonomic dysfunction. Prognostic scoring is provided by the Tetanus Severity Score (TSS), which is superior to the Dakar and Philips scores.
management: Neutralise circulating unbound toxin promptly with human tetanus immunoglobulin
Eradicate the organism with wound debridement and antibiotic therapy, metronidazole being the preferred agent
Control muscle rigidity and spasms with benzodiazepine sedation and adjuncts such as magnesium sulphate and muscle relaxants
Secure the airway and provide mechanical ventilation, often with neuromuscular blockade, for laryngeal spasm and respiratory failure
Manage the autonomic instability of severe disease with magnesium, sedation and alpha- and beta-adrenergic blockade
Nurse in a quiet environment that minimises stimuli, with intensive supportive care including nutrition and thromboprophylaxis
Administer tetanus toxoid to actively immunise during recovery, since natural infection does not confer immunity, and complete the vaccination schedule
Reinforce prevention through vaccination and appropriate wound tetanus prophylaxis in the community
